client_brief:
Cellar & Cru: Autumn shelf-talker run

Project overview
Cellar & Cru is a merchant, not a shop that happens to sell wine. We are hiring an expert to turn the supplied working files into Autumn shelf-talker run, press file plus proofs and Cellar & Cru autumn selection photography, fourteen wines at one shelf white.

What we will provide
bottle_shots/ (16 frames, 4200 x 2800); talker_2025_PRINT.pdf; autumn_list.csv; mark_card.jpg (3600 x 2400); buyer_notes.txt; bay_photo.jpg. Every file must be accounted for in the final manifest; it may be used, retained as reference, superseded, or rejected with a reason.

Scope and deliverables
- Autumn shelf-talker run, press file plus proofs: A6 portrait, one wine per page in list order, page count equal to the sellable wine count with the allocation-only lines excluded by record range, rendered at 300 ppi at trim. 
- Cellar & Cru autumn selection photography, fourteen wines at one shelf white: Sixteen supplied frames reconciled to fourteen wines and brought to one shelf white and one black point across two shooting evenings, with labels, capsules and glass colour honest to the bottle, delivered as one whole-bottle picture per wine at a settled...

Non-negotiables
- Do not invent names, prices, claims, product features, locations, credentials, records, or documentary events that are absent from the approved inputs.
- Do not silently replace a weak supplied asset. Use it honestly, reject it with a reason, or take only the brief's declared Stock or concept exception.
- Reconcile records before merge and prove page, row, name, and amount completeness from the delivered artifacts.

Working process
Please begin with an inventory and risk pass, submit the first proof or direction at the stated checkpoint, then revise against consolidated feedback. We are hiring for judgment: flag contradictions early, make the strongest defensible choice, and document any source limitation rather than hiding it.

Contract
$3,000-$7,000 fixed; target delivery 2 to 4 weeks; one direction checkpoint and two consolidated revision rounds. Final handoff includes the delivery manifest, editable sources where scoped, final exports, and a concise production note.

source_provenance.statement: The scenario is synthesized from the repository's laundered Upwork and Freelancer source anchors. It is not represented as a verbatim live listing.
source_provenance.original_anchor: Primary anchor: the recurring independent-wine-merchant brief posted on Upwork and Freelancer.com, 'shelf talkers / tasting cards, one per wine on our list', where the merchant supplies a spreadsheet of wines with region, vintage, buyer's note, score and price plus a folder of self-shot bottle photographs, and asks for printed cards that make the shelf read as one curated selection. Co-anchor: the equally common 'InDesign data merge from our printer's PDF' brief, where the client no longer holds a working file and supplies only the flat press PDF the printer produced last season, with the standing instruction to keep the artwork exactly as it is and put this season's data through it. The ledger records this slot (LAYOUT-B-13, absorbing AO-72) as a record-per-page merge with a bottle-shot column, one_line_ask 'so the shop floor reads as one curated set', and the triage verdict is STRENGTHEN: the concept, the collateral set and the price-band logic are right, but as banked the engagement sat almost entirely on the merge surface with the photography and the merchant's own mark treated as plumbing. LAYOUT-31 keeps the concept and the deliverables and restores the commission the merchant actually posts: the bottles have to be fixed, the mark has to be recovered because the original artwork left with the designer, and the point of fixing both is that the printed cards, the bay panel and the November trade tasting all come out of one selection and have to agree. No real merchant, producer, critic or publication appears; the house, its wines and its growers are coined.

real_brief_anchor: Primary anchor: the recurring independent-wine-merchant brief posted on Upwork and Freelancer.com, 'shelf talkers / tasting cards, one per wine on our list', where the merchant supplies a spreadsheet of wines with region, vintage, buyer's note, score and price plus a folder of self-shot bottle photographs, and asks for printed cards that make the shelf read as one curated selection. Co-anchor: the equally common 'InDesign data merge from our printer's PDF' brief, where the client no longer holds a working file and supplies only the flat press PDF the printer produced last season, with the standing instruction to keep the artwork exactly as it is and put this season's data through it. The ledger records this slot (LAYOUT-B-13, absorbing AO-72) as a record-per-page merge with a bottle-shot column, one_line_ask 'so the shop floor reads as one curated set', and the triage verdict is STRENGTHEN: the concept, the collateral set and the price-band logic are right, but as banked the engagement sat almost entirely on the merge surface with the photography and the merchant's own mark treated as plumbing. LAYOUT-31 keeps the concept and the deliverables and restores the commission the merchant actually posts: the bottles have to be fixed, the mark has to be recovered because the original artwork left with the designer, and the point of fixing both is that the printed cards, the bay panel and the November trade tasting all come out of one selection and have to agree. No real merchant, producer, critic or publication appears; the house, its wines and its growers are coined.
price_band_and_audience: Bottles from 14 pounds (an entry Loire white, a co-op red) to 220 pounds (a single-vineyard northern Rhone syrah, a mature Piedmontese nebbiolo). Buyer 40 to 65, a confident domestic drinker or a restaurant buyer building a by-the-glass list, who reads a shelf card the way a reader reads a review and who treats visual noise as a signal about the wine behind it. The band is load-bearing. At this tier the correct artefact is restrained and led by grower, region and vintage: generous white space, one quiet type system, the score present but small, the price plain in the run of the card, the bottle photographed straight and lifted onto a calm pale ground so the label carries. Push it toward the supermarket aisle register, price set huge, a shouting discount badge, saturated bottle photography on a dark dramatic ground, and a 220 pound bottle reads as a 6 pound bottle with an inflated ticket, which is precisely the commercial failure this merchant is paying to avoid. Push it the other way into fashion-brand minimalism where the vintage and the region are hard to find and the shop loses the one thing the card is for, which is selling wine when nobody is free to talk. A real posted job of this shape runs 1,400 to 3,000 pounds fixed, or 40 to 65 pounds an hour across 30 to 45 hours.

brand_identity.tagline: Wine worth the walk down the side street
brand_identity.sector: An independent fine wine merchant selling across the counter to retail customers and to restaurant buyers building by the glass lists.
brand_identity.founded_place_size: Established 2009, on a side street off the main shopping run in Edinburgh, Scotland. A small counter operation, one or two on the floor, an owner who buys the list himself.
brand_identity.about: Cellar & Cru is a merchant, not a shop that happens to sell wine. The owner tastes and chooses every line, and the selection changes with the season. When there is one of us on the floor and eleven people in, the shelf card is how a wine sells itself, so the card carries the grower, the region, the vintage, our note, the score and the price.
brand_identity.audience: Confident domestic drinkers and restaurant buyers aged 40 to 65 who read a shelf card the way a reader reads a review, and who treat visual noise as a signal about the wine behind it.
brand_identity.price_positioning: Independent fine wine. Bottles from 14 pounds to 220. The card is restrained and led by grower, region and vintage: generous white space, the score present but small, the price plain in the run of the line. Never the supermarket aisle, never fashion brand minimalism that hides the vintage.
brand_identity.typography: A quiet oldstyle serif for wine names and running notes, set with air, paired with a plain grotesque for regions, vintages and figures. Readable at 40 to 65, restrained rather than loud or fashionable.
brand_identity.voice: Direct, measured and honest, the owner describing a wine as if standing beside you. It says what a wine is and is not, without hyperbole. Example: A co-op red that drinks well above its price, so long as you open it an hour before.
brand_identity.brand_assets_status: The original mark artwork went with the designer who moved abroad. The only clean version we hold is a photograph of the letterpressed compliments card he had made for us, carrying the mark at about 45mm. The autumn list, buyer's notes, scores and prices arrive from the till export.
brand_identity.values: A selection chosen by one buyer with a point of view, and a shop floor that sells wine honestly even when nobody is free to talk.

assets_supplied.name: bottle_shots/ (16 frames, 4200 x 2800)
assets_supplied.kind: The merchant's own bottle photography, shot on the shop counter after closing on two separate evenings, available light plus a counter lamp.
assets_supplied.visible_description: "Most of them one evening, the rest the week after. Same counter, same camera. Together they do not look like one shelf."
assets_supplied.hidden_defect: Two faults, neither stated. The counter lamp was moved between the evenings, so seven frames sit a full step warmer and read as a different glass colour rather than a different light, and six of the wines are in near-black Burgundy or Rhone glass photographed against the dark oak counter, so a one-call knockout finds almost no luminance difference along the shoulder and bites into it, returning a clean, plausible, well-feathered cutout whose shoulder line has been cut flat and whose capsule carries a soft halo. Sixteen frames cover fourteen wines: one wine was reshot and the duplicate is not marked, and one listed wine has no frame at all.

assets_supplied.name: talker_2025_PRINT.pdf
assets_supplied.kind: The printer's flat press PDF of last season's shelf-talker, A6 portrait, one wine per page, fonts embedded, produced from the merchant's old list through a full print engine so it converts cleanly. Carries the mark, a bottle image, the wine block and a score badge.
assets_supplied.visible_description: "What the printer sent us last year. We do not have the working file and nobody here knows how it was built. Keep it as it is."
assets_supplied.hidden_defect: Two facts nobody at the shop could tell you. The system that produced the card set the entire body, grower, region, vintage, score, buyer's note, stockist code and price, as ONE continuous story with tab characters between each label and its value, so there are no per-field frames to map and every value must be driven by ordered offsets inside a single story, and the mapping readout of that story silently omits the run holding the stockist code while keeping its line break, so the string still reads as well-formed, every offset past it is short by exactly that run's length, the validator returns valid on the resulting arithmetic and the two fields sitting past the omission never become placeholders at all. Separately, the buyer's note sits in a fixed-measure frame sized to last year's notes. And the card ground, named Chalk White in the palette, is a placed warm laid stock rather than a flat process fill: rendered at trim it reproduces a measurable step warmer and slightly darker than a flat #F1ECE1 fill, so a bottle lifted onto a ground matched to the nominal swatch sits in a visible cool rectangular patch on every rendered card, a mismatch that appears only where the cutout ground meets the card ground on the rendered page and only after a card has been rendered.

assets_supplied.name: autumn_list.csv
assets_supplied.kind: Export from the shop's till and stock system, one row per line, with columns for wine, grower, region, vintage, style, buyer's note, score, score source, bottle price, case price, status and an image column.
assets_supplied.visible_description: "Our list, straight out of the till system. The notes and the scores are ours and the prices are current as of Monday."
assets_supplied.hidden_defect: Sixteen rows for fourteen sellable wines: two allocation-only lines the till still emits, flagged only by a status column the merchant never mentions. Vintages carry a leading apostrophe from the spreadsheet that exported them, the buyer's notes run from 90 to 340 characters because three were written by the owner and the rest by the part-time buyer, and the image column holds full local paths rather than bare filenames and lacks the prefix the merge's own image contract requires, so a naive run binds one bottle to every card or binds no bottles at all.

assets_supplied.name: mark_card.jpg (3600 x 2400)
assets_supplied.kind: A photograph of the shop's letterpressed compliments card lying on the counter, carrying the merchant's mark at about 45mm wide, shot in daylight.
assets_supplied.visible_description: "The only clean version of our mark we have left. The original artwork went with the designer."
assets_supplied.hidden_defect: The mark is a monoline vine-and-key device with an enclosed counter inside the key bow and a hairline rule beneath the wordmark, pressed into soft cotton paper so the strokes sit close to the paper's own texture. A knockout cannot punch that enclosed counter and collapses on the disjoint lettering, and a trace taken from a selection reads immaculately at screen scale while carrying the paper's tooth as broken edges in the hairline.

assets_supplied.name: buyer_notes.txt
assets_supplied.kind: A page from the owner describing the selection in plain language: which wines are the anchors of the bay, which two are the ones he wants people to try, and how he talks about the scores.
assets_supplied.visible_description: "How I would describe the selection if I were standing there."

assets_supplied.name: bay_photo.jpg
assets_supplied.kind: Phone snap of the shelf bay with last season's talkers in place, supplied as a feel reference.
assets_supplied.visible_description: "This is the bay. The cards sit in wooden fins in front of the bottles."

emergent_checkpoints.what_can_only_be_learned_by_running: Whether the lift actually followed the bottle. Six wines are in near-black Burgundy and Rhone glass photographed on dark oak, so along the shoulder and around the capsule the bottle and the counter carry almost the same luminance, and the knockout returns a clean, feathered, entirely plausible cutout whose shoulder has been cut flat and whose capsule drags a soft halo of counter with it. On the dark original that edge is invisible. Which frames behave that way is a property of these particular bottles under this particular lamp and cannot be read off the list, the frame previews or the glass colour alone, because two equally dark bottles separated well and four did not.
emergent_checkpoints.why_unavoidable: Ordering cannot dodge it and care alone does not either, because the tool reports success either way and the artefact it returns looks like a competent cutout until it is placed on the pale card ground and looked at. Nothing states it: the brief says dark glass on a dark counter as a description of the shooting conditions and asks for bottles lifted onto a clean pale ground, which is an ordinary client requirement, and no asset description names which six wines are at risk. It is not a propagation re-run, because the response is to abandon the one-call route for those frames and lift them instead by selecting the bottle's own material, inverting and filling to the ground, which is a different operation with a different failure mode of its own.
emergent_checkpoints.likely_rework: Re-lift the affected bottles through a material-named selection, inverted and filled to the chosen ground, checking each result on the pale ground rather than on the original. Then re-judge the whole set together, because bottles lifted by two different routes carry different edge softness and will not sit as one shelf unless the edge treatment is re-decided across all fourteen, which in practice means re-lifting some of the eight that first succeeded.
emergent_checkpoints.failure_if_undetected: Fourteen shelf cards in a bay where six of the most expensive bottles have a flattened shoulder and a grey halo, printed and stood in front of the actual bottles, in a shop whose whole proposition is that the card and the wine agree.

emergent_checkpoints.what_can_only_be_learned_by_running: What the printer's card actually exposes, and then whether the mapping built against it landed. Two things arrive only by running. First the granularity: the entire card body came out of the merchant's old system as one continuous tab-delimited story, so there are no per-field frames to map and everything must be driven by ordered offsets inside a single story. Second the yield: the mapping readout of that story omits the run holding the stockist code while keeping its line break, so the string still parses as well-formed, every offset past the omission is short by exactly that run's length, the validator returns valid on internally consistent wrong arithmetic, the placeholder step reports complete success, and the two fields sitting past the omission never become placeholders at all.
emergent_checkpoints.why_unavoidable: Granularity is not a parameter, is not reported before conversion and has no read-ahead, so the only route to it is to convert, export and read. The yield failure is worse, because it is produced by a convenience readout that presents as complete, so an agent that reads carefully and computes offsets diligently from the readout it was handed produces arithmetic that is internally consistent and wrong, and every tool downstream agrees with it. Nothing states it, since the brief says only to keep the card as it is and put this autumn's wines through it, and it is not a propagation re-run because the source of truth behind the mapping changes from a tool readout to a reconstructed story and the mapping is re-authored against it.
emergent_checkpoints.likely_rework: Reconstruct the true story by concatenating the IDML content runs, recompute every offset against that string, re-order any rows sharing a uid so their positions hold against the original text, rebuild and re-validate the mapping, re-run the template preparation, and re-verify by round-tripping IDML and grepping for every placeholder before a single card is merged.
emergent_checkpoints.failure_if_undetected: Fourteen shelf cards that bind the wine, the grower and most of the block correctly while the score and the price are silently absent from every card, printed and stood on a shelf where the price is the one field the customer is looking for, with every tool in the chain having reported success.

emergent_checkpoints.what_can_only_be_learned_by_running: Whether every buyer's note actually reaches the card. The note frame in the printer's card is a fixed measure sized to last season's shorter copy, and this autumn's notes run from 90 to 340 characters because two hands wrote them. A frame like that does not spill and does not warn: the text that does not fit simply stops rendering, so an over-long note ends mid sentence at trim and the card still looks like a finished card. Which notes are affected depends on the merged output at true trim in the printer's own type at the printer's own measure, and cannot be worked out from character counts, because the field carries a mix of wide and narrow characters and the frame's real capacity is a property of the converted document rather than of the data.
emergent_checkpoints.why_unavoidable: Ordering cannot dodge it, because nothing in the merge or the render reports an overset condition and both return success, and the truncated card is visually indistinguishable from a card whose note was simply short. Nothing states it: the brief says the notes are ours and the acceptance bar says nothing may be shortened or reworded, which is the merchant's standing requirement rather than a warning, and no earlier step measures a frame or claims to have fitted anything. It is not a propagation re-run, because the response is an escalation decision plus a change of what is bound rather than a re-run of the same binding.
emergent_checkpoints.likely_rework: Identify every truncated card by reading the rendered pages at true trim against the source note, not by counting characters. Then decide and disclose: the frame cannot be enlarged through this route and the merchant has forbidden rewriting, so the affected notes are escalated in writing before the file goes to the printer, with the shortest honest option offered (the merchant supplies a cut) and the cards re-merged and re-rendered once he answers.
emergent_checkpoints.failure_if_undetected: A shelf of cards in which the four wines carrying the owner's own tasting notes, including the two he most wants people to try, break off mid sentence at the bottom of the frame, printed, cut and stood on the shelf for a customer base that reads the card the way it reads a review.

decision_gates: The surface split: talkers to the merge surface because the layout is fixed client property and the run is record per page, bay set to HTML authoring because it needs three canvas sizes and must stay editable.
Which evening sets the shelf white, knowing a warm reference makes every white wine look oxidised across the whole bay.
How far to correct the warm evening before the correction itself becomes a glass or capsule colour the bottle is not.
Lift route per bottle: the one-call knockout is right for a pale flute and wrong for near-black glass on dark oak, and the wrong route returns a plausible cutout that reports success.
Bottle scale across the set, decided as a bay rather than per picture, and re-decided once any bottle is lifted a different way.
How to name the selection that recovers the mark: naming the card pulls the paper, naming the ink's own colour and medium pulls the mark.
Whether the traced mark is artwork or merely output, including the backing path that rides along and the size below which the hairline rule stops holding.
Whether to trust the mapping readout of the printer's own card body or to reconstruct the story independently from the document.

why_not_vlm: Paste this brief and this folder into a frontier image model and it returns pictures of wine bottles. IDENTITY: these are fourteen specific wines whose labels the customer recognises before reading a word, and a generated bottle fabricates a label, which on a card that also carries a grower, a vintage and a score is a false claim about what is in the bottle. The merchant's mark is a specific letterpressed device that must come back as the same mark, not a redrawn one, because it is already on the shop's door. SPEC: the merchant needs one card per sellable wine at A6 and 300 ppi with every field bound verbatim from their own till export, allocation-only lines absent, each card carrying its own bottle, and no delivered file larger than its source. None of that can be produced or checked by generation. EDITABILITY: two deliverables are defined by being editable, a live merge template so next season's list is a data change, and a native document with live text, a real table and real vector artwork so prices can move with the exchange rate. And the middle of the engagement is verification against material reality: did this placeholder get created, did this lift follow the glass, is this note complete at trim, is this the bottle this card names. That is not a generation problem.
